title: Va'era: fire in the hail (Exodus 9:24)
hook: fire flashes inside the hail; midrash says the two made peace to do God's will
tomorrow: Camp 4 close: you've joined the cycle

segments.voice: Yesterday, Va'era: Pharaoh's magicians, beaten by the smallest plague, said this is the finger of God. Did you admit something was beyond you? Today, the seventh plague, and two enemies working side by side. Day two hundred thirty.

Some offices have a pair like this. Two people who could not be more different. One is loud and fast; the other is quiet and careful. One is fire, one is ice. They'd never choose each other. And then the project lands on both their desks, and somehow, against every expectation, it works better than if either had done it alone. The seventh plague on Egypt is hail. Heavy, killing hail, the worst the land had ever seen. And the Torah adds a strange detail about what was inside it.
screen: `TWO PEOPLE, NOTHING ALIKE.` → `ONE FIRE, ONE ICE.` → `THE SEVENTH PLAGUE.`

segments.voice: Moses stretches his staff toward the sky. Thunder, hail, and fire running down to the ground. Then verse twenty-four says there was hail, and fire flashing inside the hail. Not beside it. Inside it. Fire and ice, in the same falling stones. Rashi calls it a miracle inside a miracle. Hail is water. Fire and water destroy each other; one puts out the other, or the other melts it away. And yet, Rashi says, to do the will of their Creator, they made peace between them. That idea runs deep in Jewish thought. An old midrash on the word for heaven, shamayim, hears in it esh and mayim, fire and water, mixed together at creation. And in the book of Job, Job's friend Bildad says God makes peace in His high places. That line, oseh shalom bimromav, the one who makes peace in the heights, closes the central Jewish prayer, the Amidah, and the Kaddish. As it's said, it's customary to take three steps back and bow to each side. One reading: if fire and water can make peace up there, maybe people can down here. One more detail worth taking home. Before the hail, Moses warns: bring your animals and servants inside. And the Torah says some of Pharaoh's own servants listened, and brought them in. Even in Egypt, some people crossed a line to do the right thing. The hail wasn't a lesson about peace. It was a disaster. But hidden in it, the rabbis found two opposites doing one job together.
screen: `FIRE FLASHING INSIDE THE HAIL.` · `ENEMIES WHO MADE PEACE.` · `SHAMAYIM — FIRE AND WATER.` · `PEACE IN THE HIGH PLACES.` · then, large: `FIRE AND ICE TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: work with someone unlike you. Settle, and breathe. Think of a person you tend to avoid working with because you're so different. The one who's all fire when you're ice, or the reverse. Name, silently, one thing they're good at that you're not. Then imagine one small task you could do together this week, each doing your part. The bell holds the time.
Va'era. The portion of the hail, where fire and ice fell together, and the rabbis said the two made peace to do God's will.
Your line: fire and ice together. Today, ask someone very different from you for help with one thing they do well. Day two hundred thirty.

howItsDone: The Amidah and the Kaddish end with oseh shalom bimromav, may the one who makes peace in the high places make peace for us, and it's customary to take three steps back and bow to the left, right and forward while saying it.

match.prompt: fire and water — tap the pairs.
pairs: they made peace to do God's will
heard as fire and water mixed
the one who makes peace in the heights

myth: the Torah says the fire fell beside the hail, not inside it
verse 24 describes fire flashing within the hail.
some of Pharaoh's servants heeded Moses's warning and brought their animals in
the text says those who feared God's word among Pharaoh's servants took shelter.
oseh shalom bimromav comes from the book of Job
in Job 25:2, Bildad speaks of God making peace in His high places; the prayers borrow the phrase.

fork.setup: you're one of Pharaoh's servants. Moses warns: hail is coming, bring your animals and workers inside. what do you do?
options: wait to see if the sky darkens.
fork.reveal: the Torah says some of Pharaoh's servants feared the word and brought their servants and cattle in. those who ignored it lost them.

original.note: Hebrew: who makes peace in His high places (Job 25:2), the closing line of the Amidah and the Kaddish.

trapdoor: what you thought: a very bad storm.
what it means: fire and ice falling together, which the rabbis read as opposites making peace to do God's will.
what a scholar hears: Rashi calls it a miracle within a miracle, and an old midrash hears shamayim, heaven, as esh and mayim, fire and water.

sources.ref: Rashi on Genesis 1:8 (shamayim as esh and mayim)

notes: Exodus 9:24 is paraphrased (JPS 1917 wording not quoted: 'fire flashing up amidst the hail' from memory, not confirmed).
Rashi on 9:24 (miracle within a miracle; fire and hail made peace to do their Creator's will) from memory; confirm.
The shamayim = esh + mayim midrash appears in Rashi on Genesis 1:8 (from Chagigah 12a); confirm.
Oseh shalom custom (three steps back, bowing left, right, forward) described generally; confirm.
Pharaoh's servants who feared the word: Exodus 9:20.

Editor review (days 226-243): Job 25:2 is spoken by Bildad, now named; 'every workplace' and 'many worshippers' claims softened to custom; the oseh shalom lesson is framed as 'one reading', not the narrator's view.
